extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, essayists, critics, and anyone interested in judgment and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles and norms from Montaigne's essay passages on judgment, experience, fortune, and vanity — guidance for how to assess people, speech, and writings. Focuses on what counts as reliable evidence of merit and how to behave in discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience must be weighed, sorted, and distilled
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough to reckon experiences; one must weigh, sort and distil them to extract the reasons and conclusions they carry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a surgeon's history of cures is useless unless he can draw from it principles showing increased skill. Travel and offices improve people only if their understanding makes that apparent; mere enumeration of experiences does not prove judgment or ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge people by outward grandeur or office alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Dignities and offices conferred by fortune are not reliable indicators of merit; titles can make men seem greater than they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man suddenly promoted appears augmented in reputation though not in merit; Megabyzus' silence before Apelles made him seem important until he spoke. The external trappings of power can mask real incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence can preserve reputation and be strategically advantageous
rubrics_metrics.description: Silence and a sullen or grave mien often procure the credit of prudence and capacity; sometimes it is better to remain silent than to expose ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: people who stand silent before those of rank are often thought great; Megabyzus received a rude reproof after speaking. Keeping presumptive knowledge by silence may preserve authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge counsels by outcomes (events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of an action does not necessarily validate the prudence of the counsel that produced it; events are a poor testimony of worth and parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Carthaginians punished bad counsel despite success; Romans denied triumphs when conduct was unfit. Fortune often compensates foolishness with success; therefore evaluate motives and means, not only result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortune, not prudence, often governs the outcome of affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Good or ill fortune are sovereign powers; human prudence cannot reliably control all causes and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and aphorisms: 'Fata viam inveniunt.' One should acknowledge the role of chance especially in public events and wars; leave some things to the gods (Permitte divis caetera).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of universal or vague judgments; require specifics and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal judgments (e.g., 'this is good' / 'that is naught') signify nothing unless one circumscribes and limits them with reasons — examine why and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cicero: examine not only what is said but what is thought and why. Demand particulars: where an opponent speaks generally, ask for the grounds and limits of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept borrowed expressions without understanding them
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people are 'rich in borrowed sufficiency' — they can utter fine sentences or quotations without grasping their force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether the speaker/reader truly understands the phrase's meaning and source. If uncertain, either challenge the point or defer to deeper examination rather than lending credit and thus bolstering ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rescue the ignorant from the consequences of their ignorance in public argument
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust and unhelpful to immediately correct or instruct someone who displays ignorance in public discourse; letting them err can expose their deficiency and prompt learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne prefers to let fools 'step deeper into the mire' so they may discern their error; immediate correction can encourage arrogance and appropriating credit ('It was what I was about to say').

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly and absurdity are not cured by bare admonition; require long education
rubrics_metrics.description: One fine admonition or lecture will not make a man wise; training and prolonged education are needed to correct folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cyrus' reply: men do not become valiant by a single fine oration any more than a man becomes a good musician by hearing a fine song. Reserve deep instruction for those in apprenticeship, not casual passers-by.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstinacy and heat in argument are signs of folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrogant assurance, obstinacy, and passionate heat in disputation are often the surest proofs of ignorance or folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most ignorant leave debates full of joy and triumph; temperament and assurance should be weighed against the quality of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence tends to leave one fearful and discontented; ignorance is confidently satisfied
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable people are cautious and often dissatisfied with their judgments, whereas the ignorant are self-satisfied and assured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psychological observation warns evaluators against equating confidence with competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: In conferences tailor your method to the opponent's strength
rubrics_metrics.description: When contending with a vigorous, clear thinker, anticipate and forestall his conclusions; with weaker minds, presuppose nothing and require explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical guidance: with strong opponents, reduce their burden by anticipating and structuring the debate; with weak ones, demand particulars and refuse to accept generalities at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: One must distinguish between what is an author's own and what is borrowed
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge the true merits of a writer, first ascertain what material and ideas are original to him and what are borrowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until one knows what is his own, one cannot fairly appraise his vigour and beauty of soul; check learned authorities to identify sources before praising an apparent wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: History should be reported more as received than as believed
rubrics_metrics.description: A historian's duty is to record what is reported by worthy people, even if he does not fully affirm it; do not suppress or over-interpret popular reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tacitus and other historians set down popular beliefs and rumours without always affirming them; historians should present received accounts and leave theological or philosophical regulation to divines and moralists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good writing should be judged on its complete, finished form, not excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a piece of work, set aside half-done or exculpatory statements ('I did it in sport', 'I never looked at it since') and ask for the perfect version the author would be measured by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the author which part they think best and judge by that; do not accept 'it was only for sport' as a reason to excuse incomplete or poor craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abridgments of good books are usually foolish
rubrics_metrics.description: Every abridgment of a good book tends to be an inferior condensation and so is generally a foolish enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of summary works that attempt to compress good originals — they often lose essential qualities and misrepresent the author's force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many celebrated works owe their fame partly to fortune, not only to merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame and reputation of books (and people) often derive from fortune and circumstances rather than intrinsic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the subject matter, timing, or patronage can make a work useful and famous even when the author gains little praise; be cautious attributing fame solely to quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of experience can be invoked to silence dissenters; interrogate its basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who cite 'I have heard, I have seen, I have done so and so' to shut down disagreement should be probed for how they derived judgment from experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand that experience be the ground of extracted principles, not mere assertion of examples; experience must show how it informs skill and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak understandings can corrupt the dignity of philosophy and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: When knowledge lodges in a weak, ill-contrived mind, it appears useless or vicious; learning requires vigor of mind to be exercised well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates' observation: weak natures spoil philosophy by handling it ill — therefore evaluate not only possession of knowledge but capacity to use it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectators and audiences are easily deceived by majesty and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: An audience often mistakes external solemnity, language, or the trappings of authority for true substance and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: grand manner and inflated language can cloud comprehension; critics should separate showy form from real content and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: One should be cautious attributing secret motives unsupported by the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not set suspicion against direct evidence; avoid imputing motives or character beyond what the facts show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne's critique of those who over-suspect historical figures (e.g., Pompey) — prefer evidence-based judgment and resist gratuitous conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep personal self-appraisal measured; people misjudge their own works
rubrics_metrics.description: People are commonly as wide of the mark in judging their own works as in judging others'; authors often misidentify the best part of their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors which part they value most and evaluate accordingly; be skeptical of self-praise and of statements that the work was only made 'in sport' or left 'half finished.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Report popular beliefs and prodigies without affirming them
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers may transcribe reports of wonders and popular beliefs but need not personally affirm them; record, rather than regulate, such beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tacitus' practice: set down what has been said by many worthy persons while disclaiming full belief; separate reporting from endorsement.
